The Long-nosed echymipera (Echymipera rufescens) is a moderately-sized peramelemorph marsupial for which considerable life-history data have been derived from closely related species due to the relative scarcity of direct field observations. For example, its neonatal wet weight is estimated at only 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams], a figure inferred from the common spotted cuscus (Spilocuscus maculatus) given the similar altricial state of newborn marsupials. Females of this species attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1200 grams [Wwi = approximately 1200 grams], though field records indicate individual variation ranging from 550 to 1200 grams, a span likely reflecting local resource availability and habitat quality across its New Guinean distribution. Males are substantially larger, with the ultimate wet weight for males reaching as high as 2225 grams [Wwi = 2225 grams]; published accounts describe a range between 700 and 2225 grams, placing this species among the larger members of its genus.

Reproductive output in Echymipera rufescens is constrained by its marsupial life history and the moderate ambient temperatures of its lowland rainforest habitat, which typically hover near 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females produce litters ranging from 1 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 4 pups per litter], with 1 to 2 litters occurring per year [F_R_i = 1 to 2 litters occurring per year]; this annual reproductive schedule yields a relatively modest recruitment rate compared to smaller dasyurid marsupials. The maximum reproductive rate is thus expressed as a combination of modest litter sizes and a restrained breeding frequency, reflecting the energetic demands of lactation in a tropical frugivore-insectivore. This pattern aligns with expectations for a medium-sized peramelemorph investing heavily in each offspring during an extended period of maternal care.

Developmental milestones in the Long-nosed echymipera have been primarily extrapolated from the closely related common echymipera (Echymipera kalubu) under captive conditions maintained at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Gestation time is notably brief for a marsupial of this body size, lasting only 13 days [tg = 13 days], a value consistent with the rapid embryogenesis characteristic of peramelemorphs at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Following birth, the altricial neonate undergoes a lengthy period of pouch development before achieving nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning is 60 days [tx = 60 days], at which point the juvenile begins to consume solid foods, although it may continue to associate with the mother for an additional period as it refines its foraging skills in the dense forest understory at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C].

Sexual maturation in Echymipera rufescens is a gradual process that occurs well after the juvenile has achieved full weaning and independent foraging capabilities. Under the typical thermal regime of its habitat at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 200 days [tp = 200 days], indicating that individuals can attain gonadal maturation within their first year of life. This relatively rapid maturation for a marsupial of its size enables the species to maintain population densities across its fragmented New Guinean range despite predictable pressures from hunting and habitat conversion. The onset of reproductive activity thus coincides with the completion of somatic growth, allowing young adults to immediately contribute to the next generation.

Metabolic physiology provides further insight into this species' ecological strategy, with direct respirometry measurements at the characteristic body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] revealing a maximum basal metabolic rate of 541 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 541 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest oxygen consumption is consistent with the low basal metabolic rates often observed in tropical marsupials, and it aligns with the species' partially frugivorous diet and moderately active foraging lifestyle. Maximum lifespan data, again inferred from Echymipera kalubu under captive conditions, indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] in protected settings, a value that, together with its early maturation and modest reproductive output, positions the Long-nosed echymipera as a classic 'slow' life-history strategist among Australian-Papuan marsupials whose persistence depends on stable adult survival rather than at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]high fecundity.
